purpose: Asenapine is used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder (also called manic-depressive illness). It helps reduce symptoms like hallucinations, confused thinking, and extreme mood swings. It can be used alone or along with other medications depending on your condition.
how_it_works: Asenapine works by balancing certain natural chemicals in your brain, mainly dopamine and serotonin. When these chemicals are out of balance, they can cause symptoms like mood swings, hallucinations, or confused thinking. By helping to regulate these chemicals, asenapine helps your brain function more smoothly and keeps your symptoms under better control.
common_side_effects: Common side effects include feeling drowsy or sleepy, dizziness especially when standing up quickly, weight gain, increased appetite, a temporary numbness or tingling in your mouth (especially with the tablet form), restlessness, and dry mouth. These side effects are often mild and may improve as your body adjusts to the medication.
warnings: This medication can cause a serious drop in blood pressure when you stand up, so rise slowly from sitting or lying down. It may increase blood sugar levels, so let your doctor know if you have diabetes. Asenapine is not safe for elderly patients with dementia-related behavior problems as it increases the risk of death in that group. Do not drive or operate machinery until you know how this medication affects you. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, as some can interact with asenapine.
typical_dosing: Asenapine typically comes as a tablet that dissolves under your tongue (sublingual), or as a skin patch (Secuado). The usual starting dose for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder in adults is 5 to 10 mg placed under the tongue twice a day. Do not eat or drink for 10 minutes after taking the tablet form. The patch is applied to the skin once daily. Your doctor will find the right dose for you based on your condition and how you respond to the medication.
